extracted.intended_audience: OSHA rulemaking stakeholders (employers, labor, occupational health researchers, public health agencies)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and methodological criteria for identifying, counting, and reporting occupational heat-related injuries, illnesses, and fatalities in surveillance and research (use of diagnostic/coding systems, data sources, denominators, exclusions, and verification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of heat-related cases using diagnostic and event codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of standardized coding schemes (ANSI Z16.2, OIICS event/nature/source codes, ICD-9 and ICD-10 codes such as 992.*, E86*, T67*, T73.2*, W92*, X30*, Z57.6) to identify potential heat-related claims, ED visits, hospitalizations, and fatalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify which code sets and code ranges were used for which time periods; combine multiple code systems when coding schemes changed over time; list codes used explicitly (examples provided in text). Manually review cases identified only by non-specific codes to ensure they are heat-related.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual/physician review to confirm heat-relatedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Review of cases flagged by codes (ANSI/OIICS/ICD) by physicians or investigators to remove miscoded records, incorrect data, burns, or cases that are not heat-related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physician review and manual inspection to improve specificity; exclude cases where diagnostic or service dates indicate the condition is unlikely to be heat-related (e.g., dehydration/kidney failure where service date is not within one day of illness date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of workers' compensation claims data and treatment of claim types
rubrics_metrics.description: Use State workers' compensation systems (State Fund, WCIS, insurance carriers, self-insured reports) to quantify heat-related injuries and illnesses, distinguishing accepted vs rejected claims and medical-only vs lost-time claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about coverage (State Fund covers portion of workers; some workers exempt or self-insured), whether analyses include rejected claims, and whether medical-only claims are included. Recognize that workers' compensation systems vary by state and influence comparability and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denominator selection and use of FTEs versus total workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of denominator (total workforce from CPS, FTEs using employer-reported hours where 2,000 hours = 1 FTE, or denominators specific to heat-exposed workers) substantially affects incidence estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible use denominators that reflect the population at risk (heat-exposed workers); report both total-worker and FTE-based rates; for seasonal analyses use quarterly or period-specific denominators (e.g., third-quarter employment/hours). Explicitly state denominator source (CPS, NIOSH Employed Labor Force, BLS QCEW) and any conversions (e.g., extrapolating NIOSH denominators to earlier years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratification by sector/industry/occupation and reporting period
rubrics_metrics.description: Report rates stratified by NAICS sector, 6-digit industry, and occupation groups and provide both annual and period-specific rates (notably third-quarter/July–September), because incidence varies widely by sector and season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sector- and industry-level rates and third-quarter rates where appropriate; present both absolute rates and relative differences (e.g., third-quarter vs annual ratios) to capture concentrated seasonal risk and differences in exposure across subsectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling coding scheme changes over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for transitions in coding schemes (e.g., ANSI to OIICS in 2005, OIICS v1.01 vs v2.01, adoption of ICD-10 in October 2015) when identifying cases across multi-year periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map and document which codes were used for which years and adjust ascertainment methods accordingly; list specific codes used for post-change periods; where necessary combine codes from multiple schemes for continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hospital ED and inpatient discharge data and determination of work-relatedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify occupational heat-related ED visits and hospitalizations using ICD codes and determine work-relatedness via expected payer being workers' compensation and/or work-related external cause codes (E-codes/Y-codes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify which codes and payer/external-cause variables were used; note limitations such as missing discharge data for some years/states, potential under-ascertainment if E-codes or payer fields are incomplete, and decisions on including residents vs non-residents and age restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions to align with denominator and data definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude populations that are not represented in the denominator source (e.g., workers under 16 years, institutionalized workers, volunteers, military) or where codes are unavailable (e.g., ICD codes not available for self-insured claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state inclusion/exclusion criteria and rationale (match CPS or other denominator definitions); document exclusions made due to missing codes or out-of-state employer locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal proximity rules for identifying heat-related medical conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Require temporal proximity between treatment/service dates and illness dates for certain diagnoses (e.g., dehydration, kidney failure) to be considered heat-related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude cases where service date for treatment is not within a short window (e.g., one day) of the illness date to reduce false positives from conditions unrelated to acute heat exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple data sources and triangulation for fatality ascertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: For fatalities, use multiple independent sources (CFOI uses at least two sources and an average of four) to identify, verify work-relatedness, and classify the event and nature of injury or illness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe source types used (death certificates, workers' compensation reports, media reports, government administrative reports) and apply consistent rules for classification (e.g., OIICS event and nature codes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting accepted-claim-only versus all-claim analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Some analyses restrict to accepted workers' compensation claims while others include both accepted and rejected claims; the choice affects incidence estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether rates are calculated using only accepted claims or all claims; if restricted to accepted claims, acknowledge medical-only claims may still be majority and that exclusion of medical-only or rejected claims changes comparability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of work-relatedness using payer field versus E-codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies determine work-relatedness either by workers' compensation as primary payer or by presence of work-related external cause (E) codes; each method has strengths and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify which method is used, consider combining methods, and note potential misclassification (e.g., cases with unknown activity or lacking E-codes may be missed when using E-codes alone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of under-ascertainment and indication of indirect heat-related injuries
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that reliance on coding (workers' compensation or heat-specific diagnostic codes) undercounts heat-related injuries, because heat can contribute indirectly to traumatic injuries not coded as heat-related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider quasi-experimental and temperature–outcome analyses to estimate excess injuries attributable to heat; compare coding-based counts to temperature-linked excess estimates to assess under-ascertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of worker self-report surveys as a complementary data source
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveys of workers (often agricultural or outdoor workers) about symptoms experienced provide incidence estimates for heat-related symptoms (e.g., sweating, headache, cramps, dizziness, fainting) over short periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use survey-derived symptom prevalences to capture non-medically-attended heat effects and near-misses; report survey time window, symptom definitions, and contextual heat exposures (e.g., heat index ranges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions about comparability across jurisdictions and data sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not directly compare rates across states or systems without considering differences in workers' compensation eligibility, data availability, coding practices, and ascertainment methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document state-specific methods and eligibility criteria; avoid combining incompatible state data into a national estimate unless methods are harmonized and coverage gaps addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion of cumulative rates to annual average and lifetime risk estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: When only cumulative rates are reported, convert to annual averages by dividing by the number of years; estimate working-lifetime risk by multiplying an annual incidence by a specified working lifetime (e.g., 45 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the assumed working-lifetime duration and clearly note that such lifetime estimates inherit the limitations of the underlying incidence estimates (notably denominator mis-specification that can under- or overstate risk).
